column1: # English words that are cousins of the French ones Weft teaches.
# The French pack shipped with no etymon and no note on any of its 587
# entries, while Old English had 544 and 126. Two of the things that make
# Weft worth using — the discoveries feed, and the "you already know this"
# line in the tooltip — are built from exactly those two fields. So for a
# French learner, the single most mass-market language in the product, both
# features were simply blank, and the marketing had to lead with Old English
# because Old English was the only place they worked.
# The French version of that story is better, not worse: a very large part
# of English vocabulary arrived from French, and most of the rest shares a
# Latin root with it. "You know more French than you think" is a truer and
# more encouraging thing to tell a beginner than anything Old English can
# Two relationships, kept apart on purpose
# DESCENT (the etymon column) is used only where English genuinely took the
# word from French or Old French. "English forest comes from forêt" is a
# claim about borrowing and it has to be true.
# COUSIN (the note column) is used where French and English both inherit
# from Latin and the English relative is a different, usually more formal
# word. cheval did not become an English word; it shares a root with
# cavalry. Writing that as a descent would be wrong, and the discoveries
# feed would then state it as fact.
# Nothing here is a guess. Where the relationship was arguable — famille and
# family both descend from Latin familia but English took it from the Latin
# directly — it was left out rather than fudged. A charming etymology that
# turns out to be false costs more trust than a blank field.
# A note must never quote the French word back at the reader. Three did:
# "route — shares a root with English “route”" is circular and says
# nothing. tools/verify-packs.mjs fails on it now.
# For descent, value is the English word. For cousin, it is the note text.
# English borrowed these from French or Old French.
# Words spelled identically in both languages are deliberately absent.
# The pack builder skips a translation that maps to itself, so the
# reader never meets them woven, and a discoveries line reading
# "fruit is simply fruit" is filler about a word that was never shown.
# Shared Latin root; the English relative is usually the formal word.
